implementation_notes: The framework generates the gateway: annotate an ordinary interface with @MessagingGateway (or declare <int:gateway>) and GatewayProxyFactoryBean creates the implementation, so business code is injected with the interface and never imports the Spring Integration API. Method calls are mapped to a request channel; a non-void return type makes the gateway listen on a temporary anonymous point-to-point reply channel, and defaults (request channel, headers, reply timeout) are overridable per method. What replaces the classic gateway class is the generated proxy plus configuration; what remains yours is the domain interface.
pitfalls: Without an explicit reply timeout the calling thread waits 30 seconds for a reply, so boundary methods should set replyTimeout deliberately.

The auto-created reply channel is anonymous and point-to-point: if another component must also observe replies, define a default-reply-channel (for example a publish-subscribe channel) and bridge it to the gateway's temporary channel.

Argument mapping follows conventions - two Map parameters, two @Payload parameters or @Payload plus @Headers on one parameter are invalid configuration and fail at startup; annotate explicitly or provide a MethodArgsMessageMapper.
An interface annotated with @MessagingGateway is not discovered by plain @ComponentScan; @IntegrationComponentScan (or importing the interface) is required.
A void return type makes the framework bind a nullChannel reply header, so replies to one-way methods are silently discarded.

variants.name: Hand-written gateway class over an AMQP client
variants.idiom_name: FibonacciRpcClient-style class: exclusive callback queue, basicPublish(replyTo, correlationId), CompletableFuture hand-off
variants.implementation_notes: Without a gateway framework the class is written by hand exactly as in the RabbitMQ Java tutorial: declare an exclusive callback queue, generate a correlation id per call, publish with replyTo/correlationId, and complete a CompletableFuture from the DeliverCallback so the calling thread can await the reply. What the framework would have generated (proxy, channel wiring, correlation table) is now your code; the advantage is zero framework dependency and full control over timeouts and retries.
pitfalls: The delivery callback runs on the client's consumer thread while the caller waits on the future - without that hand-off the call deadlocks the connection.
A dedicated reply queue per request is inefficient; one callback queue per client plus a correlation map is the documented alternative.
No timeout exists unless you add one: with no consumer running the call waits forever (the tutorial lists exactly these gaps), and a timeout still leaves the request message on the broker.
